questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Classification of Carbohydrates' refers to.
questions.a: Sugars are ranked by how many single-sugar units they carry: monosaccharides are the indivisible simple sugars fitting Cn(H2O)n, oligosaccharides join two to ten units through glycosidic bonds, and polysaccharides chain together more than ten; sugars conjugated to proteins or lipids form glycoproteins, proteoglycans and glycolipids.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Classification of Carbohydrates'.
questions.a: Count the building blocks to name the class, and note which partner the sugar carries when it decorates another macromolecule.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Classification of Carbohydrates' taught, and from which source text?

concepts.title: Stereoisomers, Anomers and Epimers of Sugars

questions.q: Using the method 'Stereoisomers, Anomers and Epimers of Sugars', work with: chiral_centres = 24. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of stereoisomers.
Take the relation taught for 'Stereoisomers, Anomers and Epimers of Sugars' and work with: chiral_centres = 12. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of stereoisomers.
Explain in your own words what 'Stereoisomers, Anomers and Epimers of Sugars' refers to.
questions.a: Every asymmetric carbon doubles the possible spatial forms of a sugar, so n chiral centres allow 2 raised to n stereoisomers; glucose alone thus has sixteen, ring closure creates alpha and beta anomers that interconvert by mutarotation, and sugars differing at a single carbon such as mannose at C-2 or galactose at C-4 are epimers.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Stereoisomers, Anomers and Epimers of Sugars'.
questions.a: Two to the power of chiral centres counts all stereoisomers; one differing carbon makes epimers, one differing anomeric carbon makes anomers.

questions.q: Write the standard relation used for 'Stereoisomers, Anomers and Epimers of Sugars', in plain ASCII form.
Using the method 'Storage and Structural Polysaccharides', work with: amylose_mid = 17.5. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of amylopectin_pct.
Take the relation taught for 'Storage and Structural Polysaccharides' and work with: amylose_mid = 17.5. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of amylopectin_pct.
Explain in your own words what 'Storage and Structural Polysaccharides' refers to.
questions.a: Long sugar chains either bank energy or build bodies: starch in plants blends about 15-20 percent unbranched amylose with the rest being branched amylopectin, glycogen serves the same fuel role in animals, while cellulose and chitin supply load-bearing walls and exoskeletons; humans cannot digest cellulose for lack of cellulase, though cattle gut microbes can.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Storage and Structural Polysaccharides'.
questions.a: Subtract the amylose fraction from 100 to price the branched amylopectin fraction of starch.

questions.q: Write the standard relation used for 'Storage and Structural Polysaccharides', in plain ASCII form.
Using the method 'Fatty Acid Notation and Unsaturation', work with: carbon_count = 80, double_bonds = 5. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of hydrogen_atoms.

Take the relation taught for 'Fatty Acid Notation and Unsaturation' and work with: carbon_count = 360, double_bonds = 75. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of hydrogen_atoms.
Explain in your own words what 'Fatty Acid Notation and Unsaturation' refers to.
questions.a: Fatty chains are written carbon-count colon double-bond-count, with delta superscripts fixing where the unsaturation falls, so 18:2 (delta 9,12) is linoleic acid; being assembled from two-carbon pieces, natural chains carry even carbon totals, and each double bond removes two hydrogens from the saturated formula.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Fatty Acid Notation and Unsaturation'.
questions.a: Decode the notation to read chain length and unsaturation; every double bond costs two hydrogens.

questions.q: Write the standard relation used for 'Fatty Acid Notation and Unsaturation', in plain ASCII form.

concepts.title: Lipid Classes from Triacylglycerol to Steroids

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Lipid Classes from Triacylglycerol to Steroids' refers to.
questions.a: Simple lipids are plain fatty-acid esters - triacylglycerols bank energy in adipose tissue and waxes coat surfaces - while compound lipids add extra groups, as in amphipathic phospholipids whose two tails and phosphate head build membranes, and steroids whose four fused rings include cholesterol, the precursor of steroid hormones.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Lipid Classes from Triacylglycerol to Steroids'.
questions.a: Ester linkages join fatty chains to glycerol; amphipathic heads-and-tails make membranes, fused rings make steroids.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Lipid Classes from Triacylglycerol to Steroids' taught, and from which source text?
Explain in your own words what 'Amino Acids and the Zwitterion' refers to.
questions.a: Each of the twenty standard amino acids is a central alpha carbon holding a carboxyl group, an amino group, a hydrogen and a variable side chain; at physiological pH proton transfer leaves the molecule dipolar - a zwitterion - and only L forms enter proteins.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Amino Acids and the Zwitterion'.
questions.a: Only the R group changes across the twenty standards; ionised plus and minus poles make the zwitterion.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Amino Acids and the Zwitterion' taught, and from which source text?

concepts.title: Peptide Bonds and Protein Structure Levels

questions.q: Using the method 'Peptide Bonds and Protein Structure Levels', work with: residues = 45. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of protein_mass.
Take the relation taught for 'Peptide Bonds and Protein Structure Levels' and work with: residues = 100. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of protein_mass.
Explain in your own words what 'Peptide Bonds and Protein Structure Levels' refers to.
questions.a: Coupling the carboxyl of one amino acid to the amino of the next forges a peptide bond with a water molecule lost at every link, so a chain of n residues holds n-1 such bonds; folding then stacks four levels - primary sequence, secondary alpha helix or beta sheet, tertiary packing with disulfide and hydrophobic ties, and quaternary assembly of subunits.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Peptide Bonds and Protein Structure Levels'.
questions.a: One water leaves per bond, so subtract one from the residue count for bonds; multiply residues by 110 Da to size the protein.

questions.q: Write the standard relation used for 'Peptide Bonds and Protein Structure Levels', in plain ASCII form.

concepts.title: Nucleic Acids and the Double Helix

questions.q: Using the method 'Nucleic Acids and the Double Helix', work with: at_pairs = 12, bp_total = 15. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of hbonds_total.
Take the relation taught for 'Nucleic Acids and the Double Helix' and work with: at_pairs = 10, bp_total = 20. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of hbonds_total.
Explain in your own words what 'Nucleic Acids and the Double Helix' refers to.
questions.a: Nucleotides - a nitrogenous base plus pentose sugar plus phosphate - string together through phosphodiester links into DNA or RNA; Watson and Crick wound two antiparallel strands into a right-handed double helix where adenine pairs thymine over two hydrogen bonds and guanine pairs cytosine over three, and heating melts the strands apart below-or-above a characteristic temperature until annealing re-pairs them.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Nucleic Acids and the Double Helix'.
questions.a: Two bonds per A-T pair and three per G-C pair let you total the hydrogen bonding holding any DNA segment together.

questions.q: Write the standard relation used for 'Nucleic Acids and the Double Helix', in plain ASCII form.
